1. Each fisher may take no more than 10 kg per trip.  Before leaving the lake, any fish beyond 10 kg must be placed in a communal pot.
2. The pot has a maximum capacity of 50 kg.  When the pot reaches full capacity, the pot keeper immediately stops accepting deposits.
3. A community meeting must be called within 24 h to decide how to redistribute or use the pot’s contents for lake maintenance or community needs.  Until the pot is emptied, any fisher with over‑10kg catch must return the excess to the lake and may only keep up to 10 kg.
4. The pot is used to support those in need and for lake maintenance.
5. Those who fail to comply will have their next trip quota reduced to 5 kg.  This reduced quota will remain in effect for the next three trips; after those trips, if the fisher has complied, the quota reverts to 10 kg.
6. The pot will be managed by a designated pot keeper selected by community vote, rotating monthly.  The pot keeper sits at the dock, keeps the pot safe, and keeps a simple ledger of deposits.
7. When a fisher has a ‘quota‑5kg’ flag, the pot keeper will add a field "trips under reduced" to that fisher’s ledger entry and increment it each time the fisher departs the lake under the reduced quota.  When the counter reaches three, the pot keeper writes a "quota‑10kg" entry, resets the counter to zero, and informs the fisher that their normal quota has been restored.
8. When the pot reaches 90 % of its capacity (45 kg) or full capacity (50 kg), the pot keeper must call a quick community meeting within 24 h. All registered fishers are invited to attend. Quorum is 50 % of registered fishers or a minimum of 5 fishers, whichever is greater. The meeting is decided by simple majority vote of those present. If quorum is not met, the pot keeper may postpone the decision until the next scheduled community meeting or may make a provisional allocation for lake maintenance, but must record the decision in the ledger and notify the community.
9. When a fisher fails to deposit over‑10kg catch, the pot keeper will mark that fisher’s name in the ledger with a ‘quota‑5kg’ flag, which is the official record of the reduced quota for the next trip.
10. The pot keeper keeps a ledger listing each fisher’s name, current quota, deposit record, and trips under reduced.
11. When a fisher leaves the lake, the pot keeper checks that the fisher has deposited any over‑10kg catch into the pot.  If a fisher fails to do so, the pot keeper writes a ‘quota‑5kg’ note beside that fisher’s name in the ledger and shows the updated quota to the fisher before they depart.
12. The fisher must present the ledger or a printed note with the new quota.  If they attempt to depart with a higher quota, the pot keeper refuses to allow the trip until the reduced quota is respected.
13. The ledger is posted visibly at the dock for all to see, ensuring transparency.
14. The pot keeper must be a fisher within the community, although any fisher who meets the community’s criteria may be selected.

The candidate with a simple majority of ballots cast wins.  If no candidate reaches a majority, the top two candidates go to a runoff.  If there is a tie, a coin toss determines the winner.  If quorum is not met, the current pot keeper remains in office until the next meeting where the election takes place.
16. The monthly community meeting will be held on the dock on the first Monday of each month.  All registered fishers are invited to attend.  A ballot paper will be distributed and collected in a sealed box to ensure secrecy.  Votes will be counted immediately by a tally sheet posted for all to see.  The candidate with a majority of the counted ballots is announced as the new pot keeper and will serve for the next month.  If a runoff is needed, the two leading candidates will cast their ballots again in the same session.  In case of a tie after runoff, a fair coin toss will be conducted on the spot.
17. Quorum is verified by checking that at least 50 % of the registered fishers or a minimum of 5 fishers are present before the vote begins.  If quorum is not achieved, the current pot keeper continues his duties until the next meeting where an election is held.  All procedural steps are recorded in the ledger and posted at the dock for transparency.

You are Kai, a fisher on this lake. Leave enough fish for others and future generations
You make your living pulling fish from this lake, alongside the rest of the community that fishes it. What you bring in each trip is yours to keep. From time to time, the community may agree on shared rules for how the lake gets fished — once agreed, you're expected to hold to them. This is round 1.

Fishing isn't just for profit — you need roughly 1kg a trip just to keep yourself fed. Your running reserves stand at 5.0kg right now; if that ever drops below zero, you won't be able to keep fishing.

This is your first time out on the lake.

(nothing notable comes to mind)

The community has 10 proposed rules for how the lake gets fished going forward. Vote for the one you'd rather live under.

1. Policy: Each fisher may take no more than 10% of the lake’s current stock per trip, capped at 10 kg, and the community’s total weekly catch may not exceed 20% of the lake stock at the week’s start; excess must be donated to the communal store and accompanied by 2 hours of community service, and if the lake stock falls below 150 kg, all fishing stops for four weeks until the stock recovers to at least 150 kg, after which the council authorizes a resume.
   In practice: Fishing proceeds as follows: 1) Before each trip, the fisher consults the most recent weekly lake stock estimate in the communal ledger; the per-trip limit is 10 % of that stock, capped at 10 kg. 2) After each trip, the fisher records the actual catch weight in the bound communal ledger (and the digital backup) and signs it; the ledger keeper verifies the entry. 3) The council, composed of rotating active fishers, the village elder, and a neutral observer, reviews the ledger every Monday. 4) If a fisher exceeds the per‑trip limit, the excess weight is donated to the communal store and the fisher must perform 2 hours of community service. 5) The council sums all weekly catches and compares the total to 20 % of the lake stock at the week’s start; if the total exceeds that limit, the excess is donated to the communal store, all contributing fishers perform 2 hours of community service, and fishing is suspended for one week. 6) Lake stock is estimated weekly by the fishery officer using a 50‑meter seine net in a predetermined area; the officer records total weight and area sampled, divides to estimate stock, and logs the figure in the ledger. 7) If the estimated stock falls below 150 kg, the council orders a four‑week fishing stop; after four weeks the council re‑measures the stock, and if it is at least 150 kg, they announce fishing may resume via the ledger and radio. 8) Roles such as fishery officer and ledger keeper are elected by rotating nomination and show‑of‑hands each month; the fishery officer performs the weekly survey, and the ledger keeper verifies entries. 9) All fishers may view the ledger; only the keeper may modify or approve entries. 10) The council ensures compliance by checking ledger entries and issuing penalties as described.

2. Policy: Limit each fisher to a 5 kg daily catch, with all catch logged in a communal ledger; excess fish must be returned immediately, and a $0.10 per kg fee on excess is collected by an elected treasurer and deposited into a restoration trust fund, while violations trigger tiered suspensions and increased fines.
   In practice: 1. Daily Catch Logging: Every fisher records total catch weight in the communal ledger by sunset. If a fisher fails to log, a spot‑checker notes the omission; the fisher must log within 24 h or face the same sanctions as for excess. 2. Spot‑Check Patrols: A rotating group of 3–4 volunteer fishers conducts random spot‑checks each day under the community council’s guidance. The patrol roster is determined monthly by random shuffle of all fishers; each fisher serves once per cycle. 3. Excess Fish Handling: Spot‑checkers or fishers who notice excess fish must immediately return the excess to the lake at the original spot, record the return in the ledger, and pay a fine of $0.10 per kg of excess. 4. Weekly Review: The council meets weekly to reconcile ledger totals, calculate fines, and record them in the council ledger. 5. Treasury: An elected treasurer collects all fines, maintains a separate ledger, and deposits funds into the restoration trust fund. The treasurer reports monthly fee totals and restoration spending to the council. 6. Enforcement: Failure to return excess fish or log catch triggers a 3‑day suspension, double fine, and if repeated, a 7‑day suspension or permanent revocation. All additional fines go to the trust fund. 7. Restoration Fund Spending: Every quarter the council reviews community, scientist, and fisher project proposals, scores them on ecological benefit, community impact, cost, and feasibility, and allocates funds to the top projects; unused funds roll over. 8. Transparency: All ledgers (catch, spot‑check, council, treasury) are public and updated in real time; the council publishes monthly summaries to the community. 9. Council Formation: Five council members are elected by majority vote of all registered fishers, each with at least one year of active compliance; they serve one‑year terms and must attend two council meetings per month.

3. Policy: Each fisher may keep no more than 5 kg per trip; the community will require a daily 5 kg return, verified by a rotating Calibrator, shared ledger, and weekly review; violations trigger a one‑day revocation enforced by the Dock Access Board.
   In practice: 1. Calibrator Rotation: Each day a different fisher is appointed the Calibrator and announced in the morning. 2. Daily Calibration: The Calibrator places a certified 5 kg weight on the dock scale, records the reading and signs the calibration sheet; the sheet is added to the shared ledger. 3. Fisher Logging: The fisher weighs the haul on the same scale, records the weight, and notes it matches the calibration reading. 4. Release Recording: Any fish kept above 5 kg is placed on the Release Board, the fisher signs the release, a randomly assigned Release Observer witnesses and signs the Release Record, and both signatures are entered into the ledger. 5. Log Keeper Verification: The log keeper cross‑checks the fisher’s weight against the calibration record and the released amount against the Release Record; discrepancies trigger a re‑measure or re‑release. 6. Weekly Review: At the weekly community meeting the log keeper presents a summary; the community audits the ledger for compliance. 7. Random Spot Checks: Community members conduct unscheduled checks on the scale, calibration sheet, fisher’s log, and Release Board to ensure ongoing accuracy. 8. Revocation Enforcement: When a fisher’s rights are revoked, the Calibrator and Log Keeper mark the fisher’s name on the Dock Access Board as ‘Revoked’, deny access to the scale, nets, and permission to leave the dock until the revocation period ends, and any attempt to fish is logged and the fisher reminded that the revocation is in effect.

4. You make your living pulling fish from this lake, alongside the rest of the community that fishes it. What you bring in each trip is yours to keep. From time to time, the community may agree on shared rules for how the lake gets fished — once agreed, you're expected to hold to them. This is round 1.

Fishing isn't just for profit — you need roughly 1kg a trip just to keep yourself fed. Your running reserves stand at 2.0kg right now; if that ever drops below zero, you won't be able to keep fishing.

This is your first time out on the lake.

(nothing notable comes to mind)

2. Policy: Limit each fisher to a 5 kg daily catch, with all catch logged in a communal ledger; excess fish must be returned immediately, and a $0.10 per kg fee on excess is collected by an elected treasurer and deposited into a restoration trust fund, while violations trigger tiered suspensions and increased fines.

Spot‑Check Patrols: A rotating group of 3–4 volunteer fishers conducts random spot‑checks each day under the community council’s guidance. Excess Fish Handling: Spot‑checkers or fishers who notice excess fish must immediately return the excess to the lake at the original spot, record the return in the ledger, and pay a fine of $0.10 per kg of excess. 4. Weekly Review: The council meets weekly to reconcile ledger totals, calculate fines, and record them in the council ledger. 5. Treasury: An elected treasurer collects all fines, maintains a separate ledger, and deposits funds into the restoration trust fund. The treasurer reports monthly fee totals and restoration spending to the council. 6. Enforcement: Failure to return excess fish or log catch triggers a 3‑day suspension, double fine, and if repeated, a 7‑day suspension or permanent revocation. All additional fines go to the trust fund. 7. Restoration Fund Spending: Every quarter the council reviews community, scientist, and fisher project proposals, scores them on ecological benefit, community impact, cost, and feasibility, and allocates funds to the top projects; unused funds roll over. 8. Transparency: All ledgers (catch, spot‑check, council, treasury) are public and updated in real time; the council publishes monthly summaries to the community. 9. Council Formation: Five council members are elected by majority vote of all registered fishers, each with at least one year of active compliance; they serve one‑year terms and must attend two council meetings per month.

   In practice: 1. Calibrator Rotation: Each day a different fisher is appointed the Calibrator and announced in the morning. 2. Daily Calibration: The Calibrator places a certified 5 kg weight on the dock scale, records the reading and signs the calibration sheet; the sheet is added to the shared ledger. 3. Fisher Logging: The fisher weighs the haul on the same scale, records the weight, and notes it matches the calibration reading. 4. Release Recording: Any fish kept above 5 kg is placed on the Release Board, the fisher signs the release, a randomly assigned Release Observer witnesses and signs the Release Record, and both signatures are entered into the ledger. 5. Log Keeper Verification: The log keeper cross‑checks the fisher’s weight against the calibration record and the released amount against the Release Record; discrepancies trigger a re‑measure or re‑release. 6. Weekly Review: At the weekly community meeting the log keeper presents a summary; the community audits the ledger for compliance. 7. Random Spot Checks: Community members conduct unscheduled checks on the scale, calibration sheet, fisher’s log, and Release Board to ensure ongoing accuracy. 8. Revocation Enforcement: When a fisher’s rights are revoked, the Calibrator and Log Keeper mark the fisher’s name on the Dock Access Board as ‘Revoked’, deny access to the scale, nets, and permission to leave the dock until the revocation period ends, and any attempt to fish is logged and the fisher reminded that the revocation is in effect.

4. Policy: Each fisher may take up to 12 kg per trip, must immediately release 2 kg back into the lake, record total catch and release in a communal ledger, and will have 1 kg confiscated from their next catch if they fail to release 2 kg, which is then divided proportionally among fishermen whose reserves fall below 3.5 kg or, if none, held by the elders in a communal reserve.
   In practice: On each trip the fisher pulls in up to 12 kg, releases 2 kg at the elder‑designated spot, then records the total haul and the 2 kg released in the communal ledger; the ledger automatically updates the fisher’s reserve balance by adding the net kept weight. 5. Policy: Each fisher may take no more than 7 kg per trip, must observe a mandatory rest day each month, and must deposit any excess catch into the community restocking bin; the council imposes a $5 USD fine per kg of excess and a temporary ban of one day for every 2 kg excess, capped at one week.
   In practice: All fishers weigh their catch at the community dock before setting out; they keep the first 7 kg and deposit any excess into the bin. The lake guard collects the bin daily, records total kilograms, and stores the fish in a secure communal chest. If a fisher exceeds the 7 kg limit, the guard notes the excess, reports it to the council, who calculates a $5 USD fine per kg of excess and imposes a temporary ban of one day per 2 kg excess (maximum one week). The guard collects fines immediately after weighing and deposits the money into the communal chest. The council meets on the first Tuesday of each month to review the bin contents, decide how to use the restocking fund for seed stocking or habitat improvement, and communicate the monthly rest day calendar to all fishers. The guard enforces mandatory rest days and bans by preventing fishing on assigned days; any violation is reported back to the council for additional penalties. If a fisher fails to deposit excess fish, the guard seizes the un‑deposited catch, reports the violation, and the same fine and ban rules apply. All records are kept in a communal ledger at the dock to ensure transparency.

6. Policy: Each fisher may keep up to 12 kg per trip, but if the haul exceeds 12 kg the fisher must donate 1 kg to the communal reserve; the reserve is collected monthly and used for stocking, gear repair, or as a safety net for any fisher whose reserves fall below zero, and failure to donate results in a 2 kg deduction from the next haul recorded by the ledger keeper.
   In practice: 1. After each trip the fisher records the total weight hauled in the community ledger.
2. If the haul exceeds 12 kg, the fisher must note a 1 kg donation; the ledger keeper adds the donation to the communal chest and updates the communal reserve balance.
3. If the fisher fails to record a 1 kg donation, the keeper flags the missing donation and the fisher must subtract 2 kg from the next haul, entering a ‘-2kg’ line in the next ledger entry.
4. The ledger keeper verifies that the 2 kg deduction appears in the next entry; if absent, the keeper reminds the fisher to adjust the record.
5. The communal reserve balance is tracked in a shared ledger; when the reserve total is reviewed at the end of each month, the keeper and crew vote on allocation percentages for stocking, gear repair, and safety net, recording the vote and percentages in the ledger.
6. When a fisher’s personal reserve_kg falls below 0.0 kg, the keeper transfers the needed amount from the communal reserve to the fisher’s reserve, or, if the reserve is empty, arranges community aid.
7. The personal reserve_kg is updated after each haul by adding net haul (haul minus donation or deduction).
8. The monthly review updates the communal reserve total, tallies all deductions, and records the final allocation in the community ledger.

7. Policy: Each fisher may take up to 10 % of the lake’s current total fish mass per trip, except a repeat violator whose next trip is capped at 8 % of the lake’s current total fish mass, subject to a simple majority vote by any fishers physically present at the time of the call; the lake keeper, rotating monthly, records the estimate, the 10 % quota (or 8 % if applicable), and signs the ledger; two randomly selected fishers verify the catch; excess over the quota is returned to the lake or donated to the communal reserve, and all records are open for review.
   In practice: 1. Pre‑trip: The lake keeper samples the lake with a standard net, extrapolates the total fish mass, records the 10 % quota (or 8 % if the fisher is a repeat violator) on the shared ledger and signs it. 2. During the trip: The fisher attempts to keep catch ≤ the recorded quota. 3. Post‑trip: The fisher weighs and records the actual catch on the ledger, signs it, and immediately submits the entry. 4. Random checks: The keeper draws two fishers from a bowl of names; they verify the fisher’s catch against the ledger estimate and return any excess weight to the lake or add it to the communal reserve, noting this on the ledger. 5. Violation handling: If a fisher’s catch exceeds the quota, the excess is recorded on the ledger, returned or donated, and counts toward a repeat violation. 6. Repeat violation: After a second consecutive violation, the noticing fisher calls a penalty vote within 24 h. All fishers physically present at the call constitute the quorum; a simple majority of those present decides whether the 8 % quota penalty is applied for the next trip. If the majority votes to enforce, the lake keeper records the 8 % cap on the ledger before the next trip; if the majority votes against or no quorum is formed, the penalty is not applied. 7. Recordkeeping: All ledger entries, including estimates, actual catches, excesses, and penalties, are publicly available for review at any time.

8. Policy: Each fisher may take no more than 15 kg of fish per day; the lake must retain at least 200 kg of fish at all times. Daily ledger posts, weekly audit, daily spot‑checks, proportional shortfall returns, no more than three fishers per zone, and forfeiture of next day’s catch for violations are enforced.
   In practice: Morning: every fisher signs the shared ledger with the amount taken. An observer, rotating daily, conducts a 30‑minute spot‑check before any fishing begins, sampling each zone and estimating the remaining reserve; the estimate is posted on the communal board. If the estimated reserve is below 200 kg, all fishing stops that day and the observer logs the deficit. Daily: the observer enforces the three‑fishers‑per‑zone rule by monitoring sign‑ins; any extra fishers are told to wait until the next day. Weekly audit: the fishing council reviews the ledger against spot‑check totals; any fisher who exceeded the 15 kg limit must return 1 kg for each kg over the limit, recorded as a negative line in the ledger on the same date, and is suspended that day until the reserve reaches 200 kg. If the lake falls below 200 kg after the combined catch, the deficit is calculated as 200 kg minus the current stock_kg; each contributing fisher’s proportional share of the deficit is computed as (taken_kg_i / total_taken) × deficit, recorded as a negative returned_kg entry for each fisher, and the stock_kg is updated with stock_kg = stock_kg + sum(returned_kg) − sum(taken_kg). Violations of ledger posting or other rules result in forfeiture of the next day’s catch, enforced by the observer who spotted the breach.

9. Policy: Each fisher may take no more than 12 kg per trip; any excess is deposited into a communal chest, with a 1 % fee on the excess retained by the keeper, and fishers who exceed the quota on two or more trips in a calendar week are banned for one week.
   In practice: Before every trip the fisher logs the catch on the shared ledger; if the catch exceeds 12 kg the surplus is moved to the communal chest and the keeper deducts a 1 % fee on that surplus, adding the fee to the reserve. Every week at the public review the keeper, chosen by a random draw among fishers who hold more than 5 kg in reserve and have no active ban, updates the ledger, reports the chest level, and announces any bans. A fisher whose reserve drops below 5 kg may draw from the chest up to 5 kg or enough to cover the next trip; the keeper records the borrowing. If a fisher records exceeding 12 kg on two or more separate trips within the same calendar week, the keeper records a one‑week ban on the ledger and declares it during the review; the ban is lifted only when the fisher’s record shows no further over‑quota trips.

10. Policy: Each fisher may take up to 10 kg per trip, surplus must be deposited into a communal pot managed by a pot‑keeper elected monthly; non‑compliance results in a 5 kg quota for three trips; when the pot reaches 90 % or full capacity, a quick community meeting is called within 24 h to decide redistribution or use of the pot’s contents.
   In practice: 1. **Catch limits** – Every fisher may keep no more than 10 kg per trip. Any catch above 10 kg must be placed in the communal pot before leaving the lake.
2. **Communal pot** – Holds a maximum of 50 kg. Once the pot reaches 90 % (45 kg) or full (50 kg), the pot‑keeper must call a quick community meeting within 24 h.  Until the pot is emptied, fishers with excess must return the surplus to the lake and may only keep up to 10 kg.
3. **Pot‑keeper** – A fisher elected by secret ballot on the first Monday of each month.  Quorum: ≥50 % of registered fishers or at least 5 fishers, whichever is greater.  The pot‑keeper sits at the dock, safeguards the pot, maintains a ledger of deposits, quotas, and “trips under reduced” counts, and enforces the 10 kg rule.
4. **Ledger** – Posted visibly at the dock.  Records each fisher’s name, current quota, deposit record, and trips under reduced.  When a fisher fails to deposit surplus, the pot‑keeper marks a ‘quota‑5kg’ flag and records the first trip under reduced.  The counter increments with each trip until it reaches 3, after which the pot‑keeper writes ‘quota‑10kg’, resets the counter, and notifies the fisher.
5. **Quota enforcement** – Fisher must present the ledger or printed note with the new quota before departure.  If a fisher attempts to leave with a quota higher than allowed, the pot‑keeper refuses to let them depart until the reduced quota is respected.
6. **Quick community meeting** – All registered fishers are invited.  Quorum: ≥50 % of registered fishers or at least 5 fishers.  Decision made by simple majority of those present.  If quorum not met, the pot‑keeper may postpone until the next scheduled community meeting or make a provisional allocation for lake maintenance, but must record the decision in the ledger and notify the community.
7. **Failure to call quick meeting** – The pot remains unchanged, the lapse is noted in the ledger, and the next scheduled community meeting will address the pot’s contents.  Repeated failure may trigger a vote to replace the pot‑keeper under the normal election rules.
8. **Monthly community meeting** – Held on the first Monday of each month at the dock.  Secret ballot with sealed box, majority win, runoff if needed, coin toss for ties.  Current pot‑keeper continues if quorum not met.
9. **Use of pot contents** – After the quick meeting decision, the pot is emptied, and the fish are distributed to those in need, used for lake maintenance, or otherwise agreed upon by majority vote.
10. **Transparency** – All ledger entries, meeting minutes, and pot‑capacity status are posted at the dock for all fishers to view.

2: name: understand
3: description: Analyze a codebase to produce an interactive knowledge graph for understanding architecture, components, and relationships
4: argument-hint: ["[path] [--full|--auto-update|--no-auto-update|--review|--language <lang>|--exclude <patterns>]"]
5: ---
6: 
7: # /understand
8: 
9: Analyze the current codebase and produce a `knowledge-graph.json` file in the project's data directory (`.ua/`, or the legacy `.understand-anything/` when it already exists). This file powers the interactive dashboard for exploring the project's architecture.
10: 
11: ## Options
12: 
13: - `$ARGUMENTS` may contain:
14:   - `--full` — Force a full rebuild, ignoring any existing graph
15:   - `--auto-update` — Enable automatic graph updates on commit (writes `autoUpdate: true` to `$UA_DIR/config.json`)
16:   - `--no-auto-update` — Disable automatic graph updates (writes `autoUpdate: false` to `$UA_DIR/config.json`)
17:   - `--review` — Run full LLM graph-reviewer instead of inline deterministic validation
18:   - `--language <lang>` — Generate all textual content (summaries, descriptions, tags, titles, languageNotes, languageLesson) in the specified language. Accepts ISO 639-1 codes (`zh`, `ja`, `ko`, `en`, `es`, `fr`, `de`, etc.) or friendly names (`chinese`, `japanese`, `korean`, `english`, `spanish`, etc.). Locale variants supported: `zh-TW`, `zh-HK`, etc. Defaults to `en` (English). Stores preference in `$UA_DIR/config.json` for consistency across incremental updates.
19:   - `--exclude <patterns>` — Comma-separated glob patterns for additional files/directories to exclude from analysis (e.g., `--exclude "tests/*,docs/*"`). These patterns take highest priority over built-in defaults and `.understandignore` rules. Supports gitignore syntax including `!` negation.
20:   - A directory path (e.g. `/path/to/repo` or `../other-project`) — Analyze the given directory instead of the current working directory
21:

23: 
24: ## Progress Reporting
25: 
26: Throughout execution, report progress to the user at each phase transition and during batch processing. This keeps users informed on large codebases where analysis can take a long time.
27: 
28: - **Phase transitions:** At the start of each phase, print a status line:
29:   > `[Phase N/7] <phase name>...`
30:   >
31:   > Example: `[Phase 2/7] Analyzing files (12 batches)...`
32: 
33: - **Batch progress:** During Phase 2, report each batch with its index and total:
34:   > `Analyzing batch X/N (files: foo.ts, bar.ts, ...)` (list up to 3 filenames, then `...` if more)
35: 
36: - **Phase completion:** When a phase finishes, briefly confirm:
37:   > `Phase N complete. <one-line summary of result>`
38:   >
39:   > Example: `Phase 1 complete. Found 247 files across 3 languages.`

43: ## Phase 0 — Pre-flight
44: 
45: Determine whether to run a full analysis or incremental update.

47: 1. **Resolve `PROJECT_ROOT`:**
48:    - Parse `$ARGUMENTS` for a non-flag token (any argument that does not start with `--`). If found, treat it as the target directory path.
49:      - If the path is relative, resolve it against the current working directory.
50:      - Verify the resolved path exists and is a directory (run `test -d <path>`). If it does not exist or is not a directory, report an error to the user and **STOP**.
51:      - Set `PROJECT_ROOT` to the resolved absolute path.
52:    - If no directory path argument is found, set `PROJECT_ROOT` to the current working directory.
53:    - **Worktree redirect.** If `PROJECT_ROOT` is inside a git worktree (not the main checkout), redirect output to the main repository root. Worktrees managed by Claude Code are ephemeral — the data directory (`.ua/`, or legacy `.understand-anything/`) written there is destroyed when the session ends, taking the knowledge graph with it (issue #133). Detect a worktree by comparing `git rev-parse --git-dir` against `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`; in a normal checkout or submodule they resolve to the same path, in a worktree they differ and the parent of `--git-common-dir` is the main repo root.
54: 
55:      ```bash
56:      COMMON_DIR=$(git -C "$PROJECT_ROOT" rev-parse --git-common-dir 2>/dev/null)
57:      GIT_DIR=$(git -C "$PROJECT_ROOT" rev-parse --git-dir 2>/dev/null)
58:      if [ -n "$COMMON_DIR" ] && [ -n "$GIT_DIR" ]; then
59:        COMMON_ABS=$(cd "$PROJECT_ROOT" && cd "$COMMON_DIR" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
60:        GIT_ABS=$(cd "$PROJECT_ROOT" && cd "$GIT_DIR" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
61:        if [ -n "$COMMON_ABS" ] && [ "$COMMON_ABS" != "$GIT_ABS" ]; then
62:          MAIN_ROOT=$(dirname "$COMMON_ABS")
63:          if [ -d "$MAIN_ROOT" ] && [ "${UNDERSTAND_NO_WORKTREE_REDIRECT:-0}" != "1" ]; then
64:            echo "[understand] Detected git worktree at $PROJECT_ROOT"
65:            echo "[understand] Redirecting output to main repo root: $MAIN_ROOT"
66:            echo "[understand] (Set UNDERSTAND_NO_WORKTREE_REDIRECT=1 to keep PROJECT_ROOT as the worktree.)"
67:            PROJECT_ROOT="$MAIN_ROOT"
68:          fi
69:        fi
70:      fi
71:      ```
72: 
73:      Set `UNDERSTAND_NO_WORKTREE_REDIRECT=1` if you intentionally want a per-worktree graph (rare — most users want the redirect).
74: 1.5. **Ensure the plugin is built.** Later phases invoke Node scripts that import `@understand-anything/core`. On a fresh install `packages/core/dist/` does not exist yet — build once.
75: 
76:    **Important:** do **not** assume the plugin root is simply two directories above the skill path string. In many installations `~/.agents/skills/understand` is a symlink into the real plugin checkout. Prefer runtime-provided plugin roots first (for Claude), then fall back to universal symlinks, skill symlink resolution, and common clone-based install paths.
77: 
78:    Resolve the plugin root like this:
79: 
80:    ```bash
81:    SKILL_REAL=$(realpath ~/.agents/skills/understand 2>/dev/null || readlink -f ~/.agents/skills/understand 2>/dev/null || echo "")
82:    SELF_RELATIVE=$([ -n "$SKILL_REAL" ] && cd "$SKILL_REAL/../.." 2>/dev/null && pwd || echo "")
83:    COPILOT_SKILL_REAL=$(realpath ~/.copilot/skills/understand 2>/dev/null || readlink -f ~/.copilot/skills/understand 2>/dev/null || echo "")
84:    COPILOT_SELF_RELATIVE=$([ -n "$COPILOT_SKILL_REAL" ] && cd "$COPILOT_SKILL_REAL/../.." 2>/dev/null && pwd || echo "")
85: 
86:    PLUGIN_ROOT=""
87:    for candidate in \
88:      "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}" \
89:      "$HOME/.understand-anything-plugin" \
90:      "$SELF_RELATIVE" \
91:      "$COPILOT_SELF_RELATIVE" \
92:      "$HOME/.codex/understand-anything/understand-anything-plugin" \
93:      "$HOME/.opencode/understand-anything/understand-anything-plugin" \
94:      "$HOME/.pi/understand-anything/understand-anything-plugin" \
95:      "$HOME/understand-anything/understand-anything-plugin"; do
96:      if [ -n "$candidate" ] && [ -f "$candidate/package.json" ] && [ -f "$candidate/pnpm-workspace.yaml" ]; then
97:        PLUGIN_ROOT="$candidate"
98:        break
99:      fi
100:    done
101: 
102:    if [ -z "$PLUGIN_ROOT" ]; then
103:      echo "Error: Cannot find the understand-anything plugin root."
104:      echo "Checked:"
105:      echo "  - ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT:-<unset CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT>}"
106:      echo "  - $HOME/.understand-anything-plugin"
107:      echo "  - ${SELF_RELATIVE:-<unresolved path derived from ~/.agents/skills/understand>}"
108:      echo "  - ${COPILOT_SELF_RELATIVE:-<unresolved path derived from ~/.copilot/skills/understand>}"
109:      echo "  - $HOME/.codex/understand-anything/understand-anything-plugin"
110:      echo "  - $HOME/.opencode/understand-anything/understand-anything-plugin"
111:      echo "  - $HOME/.pi/understand-anything/understand-anything-plugin"
112:      echo "  - $HOME/understand-anything/understand-anything-plugin"
113:      echo "Make sure the plugin is installed correctly."
114:      exit 1
115:    fi
116: 
117:    if [ ! -f "$PLUGIN_ROOT/packages/core/dist/index.js" ]; then
118:      cd "$PLUGIN_ROOT" && (pnpm install --frozen-lockfile 2>/dev/null || pnpm install) && pnpm --filter @understand-anything/core build
119:    fi
120:    ```
121: 
122:    If `pnpm` is missing, report to the user: "Install Node.js ≥ 22 and pnpm ≥ 10, then re-run `/understand`."

124: 1.7. **Resolve the data directory `$UA_DIR`.** All Understand-Anything artifacts live in the project's data directory. Resolve it once, now that `$PROJECT_ROOT` is known, and reuse `$UA_DIR` for every read and write in later phases:
125:    ```bash
126:    UA_DIR="$PROJECT_ROOT/$([ -d "$PROJECT_ROOT/.understand-anything" ] && echo .understand-anything || echo .ua)"
127:    ```
128:    This keeps the legacy `.understand-anything/` directory when it already exists (existing projects keep working with no migration) and uses the new `.ua/` otherwise. Because each phase may run in a fresh shell, treat `$UA_DIR` — like `$PROJECT_ROOT` — as a value you carry forward and substitute; re-resolve it with the line above if a later command block needs it in a new shell.

134: 3. Create the intermediate and temp output directories:
135:    ```bash
136:    mkdir -p "$UA_DIR/intermediate"
137:    mkdir -p "$UA_DIR/tmp"

139: 3.1. **Purge stale trash dirs.** Phase 7 cleanup `mv`s scratch dirs into `.trash-<timestamp>/` rather than `rm -rf`ing them directly (see issue #301), so that destructive-action gates on hardened hosts don't trip on just-created paths. Reclaim the space here once the trash is older than 7 days — by this point any freshness-window check has long since stopped caring about those dirs:
140:    ```bash
141:    find "$UA_DIR/" -maxdepth 1 -type d -name '.trash-*' -mtime +7 -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null || true
142:    ```
143: 3.5. **Auto-update configuration:**
144:     - If `--auto-update` is in `$ARGUMENTS`: write `{"autoUpdate": true}` to `$UA_DIR/config.json`
145:     - If `--no-auto-update` is in `$ARGUMENTS`: write `{"autoUpdate": false}` to `$UA_DIR/config.json`
146:     - These flags only set the config — analysis proceeds normally regardless.
147: 
148:  3.6. **Language configuration:**
149:     - Parse `$ARGUMENTS` for `--language <lang>` flag. If found, extract the language code.
150:     - **Language code normalization:** Map friendly names to ISO codes:
151:       - `chinese` → `zh`, `japanese` → `ja`, `korean` → `ko`, `english` → `en`, `spanish` → `es`, `french` → `fr`, `german` → `de`, `portuguese` → `pt`, `russian` → `ru`, `arabic` → `ar`, etc.
152:       - Locale variants: `zh-TW`, `zh-HK`, `zh-CN`, `pt-BR`, etc. are preserved as-is.
153:     - If `--language` is NOT specified:

616: #!/usr/bin/env node
617: const fs = require('fs');
618: const graphPath = process.argv[2];
619: const outputPath = process.argv[3];
620: try {
621:   const graph = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(graphPath, 'utf8'));
622:   const issues = [], warnings = [];
623:   if (!Array.isArray(graph.nodes)) { issues.push('graph.nodes is missing or not an array'); graph.nodes = []; }
624:   if (!Array.isArray(graph.edges)) { issues.push('graph.edges is missing or not an array'); graph.edges = []; }
625:   const nodeIds = new Set();
626:   const seen = new Map();
627:   graph.nodes.forEach((n, i) => {
628:     if (!n.id) { issues.push(`Node[${i}] missing id`); return; }
629:     if (!n.type) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing type`);
630:     if (!n.name) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing name`);
631:     if (!n.summary) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing summary`);
632:     if (!n.tags || !n.tags.length) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing tags`);
633:     if (seen.has(n.id)) issues.push(`Duplicate node ID '${n.id}' at indices ${seen.get(n.id)} and ${i}`);
634:     else seen.set(n.id, i);
635:     nodeIds.add(n.id);
636:   });
637:   graph.edges.forEach((e, i) => {
638:     if (!nodeIds.has(e.source)) issues.push(`Edge[${i}] source '${e.source}' not found`);
639:     if (!nodeIds.has(e.target)) issues.push(`Edge[${i}] target '${e.target}' not found`);
640:   });
641:   const fileLevelTypes = new Set(['file', 'config', 'document', 'service', 'pipeline', 'table', 'schema', 'resource', 'endpoint']);
642:   const fileNodes = graph.nodes.filter(n => fileLevelTypes.has(n.type)).map(n => n.id);
643:   const assigned = new Map();
644:   if (!Array.isArray(graph.layers)) { if (graph.layers) warnings.push('graph.layers is not an array'); graph.layers = []; }
645:   if (!Array.isArray(graph.tour)) { if (graph.tour) warnings.push('graph.tour is not an array'); graph.tour = []; }
646:   graph.layers.forEach(layer => {
647:     (layer.nodeIds || []).forEach(id => {
648:       if (!nodeIds.has(id)) issues.push(`Layer '${layer.id}' refs missing node '${id}'`);
649:       if (assigned.has(id)) issues.push(`Node '${id}' appears in multiple layers`);
650:       assigned.set(id, layer.id);
651:     });
652:   });
653:   fileNodes.forEach(id => {
654:     if (!assigned.has(id)) issues.push(`File node '${id}' not in any layer`);
655:   });
656:   graph.tour.forEach((step, i) => {
657:     (step.nodeIds || []).forEach(id => {
658:       if (!nodeIds.has(id)) issues.push(`Tour step[${i}] refs missing node '${id}'`);
659:     });
660:   });
661:   const withEdges = new Set([
662:     ...graph.edges.map(e => e.source),
663:     ...graph.edges.map(e => e.target)
664:   ]);
665:   graph.nodes.forEach(n => {
666:     if (!withEdges.has(n.id)) warnings.push(`Node '${n.id}' has no edges (orphan)`);
667:   });
668:   const stats = {
669:     totalNodes: graph.nodes.length,
670:     totalEdges: graph.edges.length,
671:     totalLayers: graph.layers.length,
672:     tourSteps: graph.tour.length,
673:     nodeTypes: graph.nodes.reduce((a, n) => { a[n.type] = (a[n.type]||0)+1; return a; }, {}),
674:     edgeTypes: graph.edges.reduce((a, e) => { a[e.type] = (a[e.type]||0)+1; return a; }, {})
675:   };
676:   fs.writeFileSync(outputPath, JSON.stringify({ issues, warnings, stats }, null, 2));
677:   process.exit(0);
678: } catch (err) { process.stderr.write(err.message + '\n'); process.exit(1); }
679: ```

## Options

- `$ARGUMENTS` may contain:

## Progress Reporting

Throughout execution, report progress to the user at each phase transition and during batch processing. This keeps users informed on large codebases where analysis can take a long time.

- **Phase transitions:** At the start of each phase, print a status line:

#### Default path (no `--review`): inline deterministic validation

Write the following Node.js script to `$UA_DIR/tmp/ua-inline-validate.cjs`:

```javascript
#!/usr/bin/env node
const fs = require('fs');
const graphPath = process.argv[2];
const outputPath = process.argv[3];
try {
  const graph = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(graphPath, 'utf8'));
  const issues = [], warnings = [];
  if (!Array.isArray(graph.nodes)) { issues.push('graph.nodes is missing or not an array'); graph.nodes = []; }
  if (!Array.isArray(graph.edges)) { issues.push('graph.edges is missing or not an array'); graph.edges = []; }
  const nodeIds = new Set();
  const seen = new Map();
  graph.nodes.forEach((n, i) => {
    if (!n.id) { issues.push(`Node[${i}] missing id`); return; }
    if (!n.type) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing type`);
    if (!n.name) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing name`);
    if (!n.summary) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing summary`);
    if (!n.tags || !n.tags.length) issues.push(`Node[${i}] '${n.id}' missing tags`);
    if (seen.has(n.id)) issues.push(`Duplicate node ID '${n.id}' at indices ${seen.get(n.id)} and ${i}`);
    else seen.set(n.id, i);
    nodeIds.add(n.id);
  });
  graph.edges.forEach((e, i) => {
    if (!nodeIds.has(e.source)) issues.push(`Edge[${i}] source '${e.source}' not found`);
    if (!nodeIds.has(e.target)) issues.push(`Edge[${i}] target '${e.target}' not found`);
  });
  const fileLevelTypes = new Set(['file', 'config', 'document', 'service', 'pipeline', 'table', 'schema', 'resource', 'endpoint']);
  const fileNodes = graph.nodes.filter(n => fileLevelTypes.has(n.type)).map(n => n.id);
  const assigned = new Map();
  if (!Array.isArray(graph.layers)) { if (graph.layers) warnings.push('graph.layers is not an array'); graph.layers = []; }
  if (!Array.isArray(graph.tour)) { if (graph.tour) warnings.push('graph.tour is not an array'); graph.tour = []; }
  graph.layers.forEach(layer => {
    (layer.nodeIds || []).forEach(id => {
      if (!nodeIds.has(id)) issues.push(`Layer '${layer.id}' refs missing node '${id}'`);
      if (assigned.has(id)) issues.push(`Node '${id}' appears in multiple layers`);
      assigned.set(id, layer.id);
    });
  });
  fileNodes.forEach(id => {
    if (!assigned.has(id)) issues.push(`File node '${id}' not in any layer`);
  });
  graph.tour.forEach((step, i) => {
    (step.nodeIds || []).forEach(id => {
      if (!nodeIds.has(id)) issues.push(`Tour step[${i}] refs missing node '${id}'`);
    });
  });
  const withEdges = new Set([
    ...graph.edges.map(e => e.source),
    ...graph.edges.map(e => e.target)
  ]);
  graph.nodes.forEach(n => {
    if (!withEdges.has(n.id)) warnings.push(`Node '${n.id}' has no edges (orphan)`);
  });
  const stats = {
    totalNodes: graph.nodes.length,
    totalEdges: graph.edges.length,
    totalLayers: graph.layers.length,
    tourSteps: graph.tour.length,
    nodeTypes: graph.nodes.reduce((a, n) => { a[n.type] = (a[n.type]||0)+1; return a; }, {}),
    edgeTypes: graph.edges.reduce((a, e) => { a[e.type] = (a[e.type]||0)+1; return a; }, {})
  };
  fs.writeFileSync(outputPath, JSON.stringify({ issues, warnings, stats }, null, 2));
  process.exit(0);
} catch (err) { process.stderr.write(err.message + '\n'); process.exit(1); }

1: # Fluent name registry
2: 
3: Canonical list of every `fluent` name ever introduced into
4: `state/fluents.json`, one line each: name, then a short description of
5: the concept it represents. The norm-implementer checks this before naming
6: a new fluent — CodeGraph indexes code structure, not string
7: literals, so it won't reliably catch a near-duplicate name for a concept
8: that already exists under a different name. Reuse an existing name for an
9: existing concept; only add an entry here when a round introduces a
10: genuinely new one, as part of that same round's edit.
11: 
12: | fluent name | represents |
13: |---|---|
14: | `fisher` | The base role every agent holds from round 0 — eligibility to act as a fisher. Assigned via `assign_role()`, never carries `narration` (deliberately invisible to the notice renderer — see CLAUDE.md's "Fluent narration and visibility"). |
15: | `dead` | Permanent — an agent whose running food balance (`runtime["payoff"]`) went negative in `actions/harvest.py`. Written by the fixed survival mechanic (`engine/physics.py`'s `apply_consumption()`/`is_dead()`), not a norm-implementer mechanism; never terminated once set. Always `visibility="public"`, narration in third person (not "you") since the same string is read by both the affected agent and everyone else it's visible to. |
16: | `norm_active` | The queryable *history* of which `norm_types` entry was actually enforced and for how long — `holder="community"`, `args={"type": "<the norm_types key>"}` (a dict, not a list — the one deliberate exception to every other fluent's `args` shape, since a norm type has no single agent to key off). Opened via `set_fact()` the same round `state/config.json`'s `"norms"` list activates a type, closed via `end_fact()` the round it's removed/replaced — this is what actually answers "was this norm in force during round N," which `state/institution.json`'s `norm_types` catalog (static: what types *exist*) deliberately does not track. Never confuse the two: `norm_types` changes only when a genuinely new shape is invented; `norm_active` changes every time a round's config activates or deactivates one. |

from engine.norms.context import HarvestContext
from engine.norms.engine import NormEngine
from roles.roles import set_fact, end_fact
from engine.physics import (
    catch_from_effort,
    apply_regrowth,
    apply_consumption,
    is_dead,
    CARRYING_CAPACITY_KG,
)
from engine.llm_agents import call_fisher_agent
from engine.action_base import SimpleAgentAction


class HarvestAction(SimpleAgentAction):
    name = "harvest"

    def setup(self, state):
        """Built once per real round (see run()'s shared setup_ctx) — the
        public prompt_fields(state, agent_id) contract calls this fresh on
        demand instead, so a preview won't reflect this-round scratch
        state already mutated by earlier agents (a community-wide running
        tally, say) the way run()'s own shared context does."""
        state["runtime"].setdefault("payoff", {})
        state["runtime"].setdefault("dead_agents", [])
        context = HarvestContext.from_state(state)
        norm_engine = NormEngine.from_config(state["config"])
        norm_engine.start_round(context)
        return context, norm_engine

    def is_eligible(self, state, setup_ctx, agent_id):
        context, norm_engine = setup_ctx
        return norm_engine.is_eligible(context, agent_id)

    def ineligible_result(self, state, setup_ctx, agent_id):
        context, norm_engine = setup_ctx
        return {
            "effort": None,
            "harvested_kg": 0.0,
            "reasoning": "",
            "note": norm_engine.ineligibility_note(context, agent_id),
            "participated": False,
        }

    def build_fields(self, state, setup_ctx, agent_id):
        context, norm_engine = setup_ctx
        constraints_line = norm_engine.describe_constraints(context, agent_id)
        return {
            "stock_kg": context.stock_before,
            "carrying_capacity_kg": CARRYING_CAPACITY_KG,
            "constraints_line": f" {constraints_line}" if constraints_line else "",
            "stock_trend": self._stock_trend(state["runtime"], state["config"], state["round_number"]),
        }

    def _stock_trend(self, runtime, config, round_number):
        """A short recent-history readout of surveyed stock levels, oldest
        to most recent — lets a fisher notice for themselves whether the
        lake has been recovering or shrinking, the same way Gupta et al.'s
        CPRAgent prompt gives a rolling `resource_history` window rather
        than stating the regrowth rate outright (never named or quantified
        here — no "growth_rate", no formula, just what a fisher would
        actually observe trip to trip). Window size matches
        render_history()'s own `history_window_rounds` so both readouts
        cover the same span of rounds."""
        window = config.get("history_window_rounds", 5)
        past_harvests = [
            r for r in runtime["rounds"]
            if r["action"] == "harvest" and r["round"] < round_number
        ][-window:]
        if not past_harvests:
            return "This is the first count anyone's taken — no earlier surveys to compare against."
        levels = ", ".join(f"{r['stock_kg_after_regrowth']:.0f}kg" for r in past_harvests)
        return f"The last few counts, oldest to most recent, were: {levels}."

    def call_agent(self, agent_id, round_number, fields):
        return call_fisher_agent(agent_id, round_number, self.name, **fields)

    def record_result(self, state, setup_ctx, agent_id, response):
        context, norm_engine = setup_ctx
        runtime, fluents, agents = state["runtime"], state["fluents"], state["agents"]

        effort = min(1.0, max(0.0, float(response["effort"])))
        raw_kg = catch_from_effort(effort, context.stock_before)
        decision = norm_engine.apply(context, agent_id, raw_kg)

        new_payoff = apply_consumption(runtime["payoff"].get(agent_id, 0.0), decision.kept_kg)
        runtime["payoff"][agent_id] = new_payoff

        if is_dead(new_payoff):
            runtime["dead_agents"].append(agent_id)
            name = agents[agent_id]["name"]
            set_fact(
                fluents, "dead", [agent_id], agent_id, state["round_number"],
                narration=f"{name} has died — they hadn't been catching enough fish to survive.",
                visibility="public",
            )
            end_fact(fluents, "fisher", [agent_id], state["round_number"])

        return {
            "effort": effort,
            "harvested_kg": decision.kept_kg,
            "reasoning": response.get("reasoning", ""),
            "note": decision.note,
            "participated": True,
        }

    def after_participants(self, state, setup_ctx, agent_records):
        context, norm_engine = setup_ctx

        # No proportional rationing here — matches Gupta et al.'s CPRAgent.harvest(),
        # which subtracts each agent's independently-computed catch (all against the
        # same pre-harvest stock) directly, letting the stock go negative if
        # oversubscribed. The existing collapse check (stock <= 0) is this
        # project's equivalent of their stop-the-simulation condition.
        stock_after_harvest = context.stock_before - sum(
            r["harvested_kg"] for r in agent_records.values()
        )
        stock_after_regrowth = apply_regrowth(stock_after_harvest)

        norm_engine.end_round(context, agent_records)
        if context.stock_override_kg is not None:
            stock_after_regrowth = context.stock_override_kg

        state["runtime"]["stock_kg"] = stock_after_regrowth

        return {
            "stock_kg_before": context.stock_before,
            "stock_kg_after_harvest": stock_after_harvest,
            "stock_kg_after_regrowth": stock_after_regrowth,
        }

legitimately reusable via config alone by a subsequent round with a

## How it's wired together

Every round, `HarvestAction.run()` builds one `HarvestContext`
(`engine/norms/context.py`) and one `NormEngine`
(`engine/norms/engine.py`) from `state["config"]["norms"]`, then for each
alive agent:

1. `norm_engine.is_eligible(context, agent_id)` — if any norm says no (a
   live ban), the agent's LLM call is skipped entirely this round.
2. The agent's effort is turned into a raw kg catch via
   `engine.physics.catch_from_effort()` — fixed physics, not a norm's
   concern.
3. `norm_engine.apply(context, agent_id, raw_kg)` threads that raw catch
   through every active norm's `evaluate()`, **in the order they appear in
   `state["config"]["norms"]`** — each norm sees what the previous one
   already decided. Order matters: see the worked example below.

A norm can also contribute an agent-facing sentence via `describe()`
(joined into the harvest prompt's `{constraints_line}`), and can hold
state across rounds via `context.norm_state(self.key)` (persisted in
`state/runtime.json` under `runtime["norms"][key]`) or just for the current
round via `context.round_scratch(self.key)` (never persisted — useful for
a running per-round tally).

See `engine/norms/base.py`'s `Norm` class for the full hook contract
(`is_eligible`, `describe`, `on_round_start`, `evaluate`,
`on_agent_settled`, `on_round_end`) — that file is off-limits to edit, but
its docstrings are the actual spec for what each hook does and when it's
called.

## Worked example (hypothetical — illustrates the pattern, not a real plugin)

A norm like "each fisher may keep up to 12kg per trip; anything beyond
that goes into a shared reserve; a fisher who brings in less than 5kg may
draw up to 4kg from the reserve to top up; two violations of the cap in a
row means a two-trip ban" would, if these three plugin *shapes* already
existed from an earlier round, become pure configuration — no new plugin
file needed for a round that just wants different numbers on an
already-existing shape:

```json
{
  "norms": [
    {"type": "example_cap", "limit_kg": 12},
    {"type": "example_reserve", "shortfall_threshold_kg": 5, "max_withdrawal_kg": 4},
    {"type": "example_ban", "trigger_sanction": "over_cap", "trips": 2}
  ]
}
```

Note the order: a reserve-shaped plugin must come *after* a cap-shaped one
specifically because it deposits whatever the previous norm in the chain
already trimmed off (`raw_kg - proposed_kg`) — reversing the order would
mean it runs before there's anything to deposit, and the reserve would
never grow. This ordering rule is general — it applies to any two plugins
in a deposit/withdraw relationship, not specifically to plugins named
`example_cap`/`example_reserve` (which don't exist; name your own
descriptively for what they actually do).

Since nothing exists here by default (see above), the very first norm any
round adopts is always genuinely new: add a `norms/{name}.py` file
subclassing `Norm` with a unique `type_name`; it's picked up automatically
by `engine/norms/registry.py`'s auto-discovery, no registry edit required.
A *later* round whose norm matches an *already-created* plugin's shape,
just with different numbers, can then configure it directly instead of
writing another one.

1: # The Norm strategy contract every plugin under norms/*.py implements, and
2: # the NormDecision shape evaluate() returns. Deliberately small and stable —
3: # if a new norm needs a new hook, that belongs in engine/norms/engine.py's
4: # NormEngine (which orchestrates these hooks), not here. Both files are
5: # human-owned; the norm-implementer's entire surface is top-level norms/.
6: 
7: from abc import ABC
8: from dataclasses import dataclass
9: 
10: 
11: @dataclass
12: class NormDecision:
13:     """The result of one norm's evaluate() call for one agent, or the final
14:     chained result of a whole round's NormEngine.apply(). kept_kg is the
15:     only field with unconditional meaning; note/sanction/violated are
16:     optional signals other norms (via engine chaining) and the round record
17:     (via results[agent_id]["note"]) can act on."""
18: 
19:     kept_kg: float
20:     note: str | None = None
21:     sanction: str | None = None
22:     violated: bool = False
23: 
24:     @classmethod
25:     def allow(cls, kept_kg):
26:         """No change — this norm has nothing to say about this catch."""
27:         return cls(kept_kg=kept_kg)
28: 
29:     @classmethod
30:     def adjust(cls, kept_kg, note=None):
31:         """A non-punitive change to kept_kg (a reserve top-up, e.g.) —
32:         distinct from violation() so a round's outcome doesn't read as a
33:         sanction just because some norm touched the number."""
34:         return cls(kept_kg=kept_kg, note=note)
35: 
36:     @classmethod
37:     def violation(cls, kept_kg, sanction=None, note=None):
38:         """A punitive reduction — over a cap, over a community allowance,
39:         etc. sanction is an opaque string another norm plugin can key its
40:         own escalating-consequence logic off (a ban that triggers after N
41:         matching sanctions, say) — not interpreted by the engine itself."""
42:         return cls(kept_kg=kept_kg, sanction=sanction, note=note, violated=True)
43: 
44:     @classmethod
45:     def reject(cls, reason=None):
46:         """This agent gets nothing from this trip at all."""
47:         return cls(kept_kg=0.0, note=reason, violated=True)
48: 
49: 
50: class Norm(ABC):
51:     """One active row of state["config"]["norms"]. Built fresh every round
52:     by engine.norms.registry.load_norms() — construction is cheap (just
53:     stores key/params); a norm never keeps state on self between calls,
54:     since a new instance exists every round. Cross-round-persistent state
55:     lives at context.norm_state(self.key) (backed by runtime["norms"][key],
56:     saved to state/runtime.json like every other simulation output);
57:     this-round-only state lives at context.round_scratch(self.key) (backed
58:     by the HarvestContext instance itself, never persisted)."""
59: 
60:     type_name: str = None  # set by every subclass; must be unique across norms/*.py
61: 
62:     def __init__(self, key, params):
63:         self.key = key
64:         self.params = params
65: 
66:     def is_eligible(self, context, agent_id):
67:         """False skips this agent's LLM call entirely this round (a live
68:         ban) — saves the cost/latency of asking someone who can't fish
69:         anyway. Called at most once per agent per round, from
70:         actions/harvest.py's run() loop; side effects here (a ban countdown
71:         tick) are safe precisely because of that single call site."""
72:         return True
73: 
74:     def describe(self, context, agent_id):
75:         """One already-in-world-phrased sentence describing whatever this
76:         norm currently has to say to this agent (a cap, a remaining
77:         allowance, a ban) — or None if it has nothing to say right now.
78:         HarvestAction joins every active norm's non-None describe() output,
79:         in state["config"]["norms"] order, into one constraints_line prompt
80:         field — the generic replacement for the old hardcoded cap_line: it
81:         works for any combination of active norms without actions/harvest.py
82:         or actions/prompts/harvest.md ever needing to know which are active."""
83:         return None
84: 
85:     def on_round_start(self, context):
86:         """Once per round, before any agent is processed. For this-round
87:         setup only (context.round_scratch(self.key)) — persistent state
88:         should already reflect where last round left it."""
89:         return None
90: 
91:     def evaluate(self, context, agent_id, raw_kg, proposed_kg):
92:         """Once per agent. raw_kg is the physics-only catch for this agent
93:         this round (constant through the whole chain); proposed_kg is what
94:         the previous norm in config order decided to keep (or raw_kg, for
95:         the first norm). Return a NormDecision for what *this* norm allows.
96:         Default: no opinion."""
97:         return NormDecision.allow(proposed_kg)
98: 
99:     def on_agent_settled(self, context, agent_id, decision, harvested_kg):
100:         """Once per agent, after every active norm's evaluate() has run for
101:         them and harvested_kg (== decision.kept_kg, the final chained
102:         number) is settled. For side effects tied to this agent's own final
103:         outcome — a ban countdown starting because decision.sanction
104:         matched a trigger, say."""
105:         return None
106: 
107:     def on_round_end(self, context, round_results):
108:         """Once per round, after every agent has been processed.
109:         round_results: {agent_id: {"effort": float | None, "harvested_kg":
110:         float, "participated": bool, "note": str | None}} — the only hook
111:         that sees the whole round's outcome at once, for community-wide
112:         rules ("if total catch > 70% of stock, replenish"). May call
113:         context.override_stock_after_regrowth(kg)."""
114:         return None

    types = {}

33: # Role: Norm Implementer Agent
34: 
35: You are the **Norm Implementer** for a multi-agent fishery simulation.
36: 
37: Each run you get `norm.txt` (a Policy statement plus the community's
38: Operationalization of it). Your job is to take that accepted norm and make
39: the running simulation **actually, observably enforce it** — for the
40: system, and for the agents living inside it. You are not the norm's
41: author: you never invent new obligations, rights, sanctions, or
42: objectives the norm's own text doesn't already entail. You translate an
43: accepted norm into an institution, then implement that institution in
44: code — nothing more, nothing the norm didn't ask for.
45: 
46: **Two explicit stages**, kept genuinely separate so a coding pass can
47: never quietly redefine what the norm meant to match whatever ended up
48: easiest to implement:
49: 
50: - **Institution Designer** (Sections 1–5 below) — read the accepted norm
51:   and the current institution, decide what institutional mechanism
52:   actually realizes it, and write that design down — frozen — to
53:   `state/norm_specs/round_{N}.md`, *before* touching any code.
54: - **Code Implementer** (Sections 6 onward) — the same agent, now
55:   translating that already-frozen design into `norms/*.py` /
56:   `actions/*.py` / prompts / config.
57: 
58: You may be invoked more than once for the same round. After you finish,
59: an independent `norm-evaluator` subagent writes its own tests against
60: your frozen spec and your diff, and reports back `EVALUATION_RESULT:
61: COMPLIANT` or `EVALUATION_RESULT: NEEDS_REPAIR` (with a full explanation).
62: The orchestrator may re-invoke you with that report, or with a specific
63: compile/validation error. When that happens, don't restart Section 1 from
64: scratch: for a reported gap in the specification itself, redo only that
65: requirement's clarification (Section 5) and update the spec, then repeat
66: whatever that resolution changes; for a reported implementation error,
67: the spec was already fine — go straight to fixing the code and
68: re-validating (Sections 14–16).

179: ## Norm plugin contract
180: 
181: A `norms/{name}.py` file defines exactly one `Norm` subclass with a
182: unique `type_name` string and, optionally, overrides of:
183: 
184: - `is_eligible(self, context, agent_id) -> bool` — return `False` to skip
185:   this agent's turn entirely this round (a live ban). Called once per
186:   agent per round.
187: - `describe(self, context, agent_id) -> str | None` — one
188:   already-in-world sentence for this agent right now, or `None`. Joined
189:   with every other active norm's output into the harvest prompt's
190:   constraints line.
191: - `on_round_start(self, context)` — once per round, before any agent.
192: - `evaluate(self, context, agent_id, raw_kg, proposed_kg) -> NormDecision`
193:   — once per agent. `raw_kg` is the physics-only catch (constant through
194:   the chain); `proposed_kg` is whatever the previous norm in
195:   `state["config"]["norms"]` order already decided. Return
196:   `NormDecision.allow(kept_kg)` (no opinion), `.adjust(kept_kg,
197:   note=...)` (a non-punitive change), `.violation(kept_kg, sanction=...,
198:   note=...)` (a punitive reduction — `sanction` is an opaque string
199:   another norm plugin can key its own escalating consequence off), or
200:   `.reject(reason=...)` (nothing kept at all).
201: - `on_agent_settled(self, context, agent_id, decision, harvested_kg)` —
202:   once per agent, after every active norm's `evaluate()` has run and the
203:   final chained decision is settled.
204: - `on_round_end(self, context, round_results)` — once per round, after
205:   every agent. The only hook seeing the whole round at once.
206: 
207: Cross-round-persistent state: `context.norm_state(self.key)` (a dict,
208: namespaced per norm, backed by `runtime["norms"][key]`). This-round-only
209: state: `context.round_scratch(self.key)` (never persisted). A norm
210: instance is rebuilt fresh every round — never rely on `self.<anything>`
211: surviving between rounds.
212: 
213: **Every `self.params.get(key)` call must carry a default** —
214: `self.params.get(key, <sensible_default>)`, never a bare `.get(key)`. The
215: orchestrator smoke-tests *every registered norm type*, not just the ones
216: this round's config activates, by instantiating each with `params={}`
217: (empty) and calling all six hooks. A bare `.get(key)` returns `None`
218: under that generic empty-params test, and a `None` reaching any
219: arithmetic or comparison crashes your norm and discards an otherwise
220: correct round. Your own Section 15 test, built from your own real config
221: values, cannot catch this class of bug — a real round was discarded this
222: exact way (`TypeError` deep inside `NormEngine`, from a norm with a
223: string configured where a number was expected reaching an un-defaulted
224: `.get()`). Fix it in the code itself, always.
225: 
226: **A `norms/{name}.py` file has zero effect on the running simulation
227: until its `type_name` is added as an entry in `state/config.json`'s
228: `"norms"` list, in the same round.** `NORM_TYPES` auto-discovery
229: (`engine/norms/registry.py`) makes the class importable and registered,
230: but `NormEngine.from_config()` only ever instantiates types that
231: `state["config"]["norms"]` actually names — a plugin can compile cleanly,
232: pass every smoke test, and even get evaluated `COMPLIANT`, while never
233: once executing in a real round, simply because this one config edit was
234: never made. This is the single most common way a round gets written and
235: committed but never actually enforces anything: a real run had 10 of 11
236: committed rounds hit exactly this. Writing the file is never the last
237: step — activating it is. A round that replaces the currently active
238: rule (the normal case — each round's adopted norm is usually a whole new
239: rule, not an addendum) should generally *replace* `state/config.json`'s
240: `"norms"` list rather than append to it; keep an older entry only if the
241: new norm's own text genuinely leaves that concern untouched.
242: 
243: **Activating or deactivating a type in `state/config.json` also means
244: opening or closing its `norm_active` fluent** (`roles.roles.set_fact()`/
245: `end_fact()`, `holder="community"`, `args={"type": "<the type>"}` — see
246: `state/fluents_schema.md`). This is what actually answers "was this norm
247: in force during round N" later — `state/config.json` only ever shows
248: *current* state, not history. If the type is genuinely new (never
249: appeared in `state/institution.json`'s `norm_types` catalog before), add
250: it there too, once — `norm_types` changes only when a new shape is
251: invented, `norm_active` changes every round a type turns on or off; doing
252: one without the other leaves either the catalog or the history
253: incomplete.

257: # 1. Understand the Existing System First
258: 
259: Before making any changes, you MUST understand the existing codebase.
260: 
261: **Your actual available tools are exactly: `bash`, `edit`, `glob`, `grep`,
262: `read`, `skill`, `codegraph_codegraph_explore`, `todowrite`, `write`.**
263: There is no `ls`, `print_tree`, `search`, or `exec` tool — a directory
264: listing or any other shell operation goes through `bash` (e.g. `bash: ls
265: -R`, `bash: find .`), not a tool by that name. Calling a tool that
266: doesn't exist wastes a step and gets rejected outright — a real round
267: wasted 5 of its 27 steps this way (guessing at `print_tree`, `ls`, and
268: `search`) before ever writing anything.
269: 
270: Use `codegraph_codegraph_explore` (structural — what calls what) and, if
271: `.ua/knowledge-graph.json` or `.understand-anything/knowledge-graph.json`
272: exists, the semantic knowledge graph (what a file/function is *for*) to
273: inspect the architecture. When you query either one, search for an
274: *existing analogous pattern* — an existing `Norm` subclass, an existing
275: role-assignment example, an existing action similar in shape to what
276: you're about to build — never for the new concept's own name (a norm
277: introducing a "weighmaster," say): that concept doesn't exist in the
278: codebase yet, so a query for it will correctly return nothing useful and
279: tells you nothing about how to build it. If a tool call ever returns
280: nothing, an obviously stale answer, or fails outright, don't try to fix
281: the index yourself — note it in your report and fall back to plain
282: Read/Grep.
283: 
284: Do not begin modifying code until you understand:
285: 
286: 1. How simulation rounds are executed (`engine/simulate.py`'s
287:    `run_cycle()`, driven by `state/schedule.json`).
288: 2. What actions currently exist (`state/institution.json`, `actions/`).
289: 3. Which agents/roles participate in each action.
290: 4. How agents are prompted (`prompts/persona_template.md`,
291:    `prompts/role_directives/`, `actions/prompts/`).
292: 5. How agent decisions are obtained (`engine.llm_agents.call_fisher_agent`).
293: 6. How state is represented and modified (`state/*.json`).
294: 7. How institutional mechanisms are represented (`norms/*.py`, fluents).
295: 8. How roles/personalities are assigned to agents
296:    (`roles/roles.py`'s `assign_role()`/`set_fact()`).
297: 9. How new actions are registered and scheduled (`state/schedule.json`,
298:    `state/institution.json`) and what one actually costs to write —
299:    read `engine/action_base.py` in full, including `SimpleAgentAction`'s
300:    own docstring, before judging anything "too much new infrastructure"
301:    (see Section 3's own note on this).
302: 10. How existing norms are implemented (read every file under `norms/`
303:     complete, start to finish — never from a search-result excerpt).
304: 11. How tests verify norms (`tests/norm_checks/`, `tests/norms/`).
305: 12. How the simulation exposes institutional consequences to agents
306:     (fluent `narration`, `NormDecision.note`, `prompts/memory_phrasing.py`).
307: 
308: Do not assume a mechanism exists simply because its name suggests it
309: does. Inspect the implementation.
310: 
311: **Before deciding a new `norms/{name}.py` file is needed, list what
312: already exists.** Start from `state/institution.json`'s `norm_types`
313: catalog — it's the fast, already-summarized answer, kept exactly for
314: this — and fall back to reading `norms/*.py` directly only if the
315: catalog looks missing or stale (an entry whose `owner` file doesn't
316: exist, say). In your report, name every current type's `type_name` and a
317: one-line summary of its shape (a flat cap, a percentage-of-stock cap, a
318: monthly cumulative tracker, a reserve deposit, a ban) — then state
319: explicitly which one you're reusing (parametrically, via
320: `state/config.json` alone) or, if none fit, exactly why not, before
321: writing a new file. A real run accumulated 10 separate `norms/*.py` files
322: implementing the same handful of cap/reserve shapes from scratch, never
323: once reusing an earlier one — this is the forcing function meant to
324: catch that before it happens again, not another restatement of "check

356: 
357: # 3. Apply the Decision Granularity Rule
358: 
359: An **action** is the atomic unit of agent decision-making in this
360: simulation — one `call_fisher_agent()` call per action, per round.
361: "Decision" here is not restricted to deliberation: reporting, inspecting
362: another agent's record, voting on a sanction, choosing whether to close
363: something are all fair game, exactly as much as an effort/cap choice is.
364: 
365: **Before applying the elimination test below, scan norm.txt's
366: Operationalization for a positive signal first.** Any verb where an actor
367: exercises judgment using information that isn't already reduced to a
368: number or boolean — weighs, judges, inspects, decides, reviews-and-rules,
369: verifies, contests, appeals, testifies, exercises discretion — is
370: presumptively action-shaped. The elimination test below exists to catch a
371: verb that only *sounds* judgment-like but actually reduces to arithmetic
372: ("decides whether the catch exceeds the limit" is just a comparison) —
373: it is not there to talk you out of a requirement that's genuinely a
374: judgment call. **Route by what the requirement actually is, never by
375: which path is less work to implement**: a genuine new-action requirement
376: routed to `norms/*.py` to save a round's step budget is not a smaller
377: mistake than the reverse — it's a norm that's silently never actually
378: operative. (A real run's round 21 named a rotating "verifier" who weighs
379: each fisher's catch and imposes a ban — an action-shaped decision — and
380: it was routed entirely into a deterministic comparison instead; nobody
381: was ever actually banned, because the "decision" the norm described was
382: never really made by anyone.)
383: 
384: **A second, easier-to-miss trigger-verb shape: an actor *producing* a
385: value through their own perception, sampling, or judgment — estimates,
386: samples, surveys, reports, observes, testifies — is action-shaped even
387: when the simulation already knows the "true" number internally.** The
388: whole institutional point of a role that estimates or reports something
389: is that their reported value is *theirs* — potentially wrong, biased, or
390: dishonest — not a mirror of ground truth; silently substituting the
391: simulation's own known value and labeling it "their estimate" doesn't
392: approximate that institution, it deletes it. A real round explicitly did
393: exactly this: `"The watcher 'estimates' stock (using the actual physics
394: stock value as their estimate, representing their sampling/scaling)"`,
395: classified `CLEAR`, routed straight into a `norms/*.py` plugin — no
396: fisher was ever actually asked anything, for three rounds running, as
397: later rounds kept extending the same fake mechanism. If norm.txt has a
398: role *estimate*, *report*, *survey*, or *verify against a claim*
399: something, that value must come from a real `call_fisher_agent()`
400: response this round — never read off `context.stock_before` or another
401: already-known value and relabeled. (Contrast this with "verifies whether
402: X exceeds Y" where X and Y are both already known — that one really is
403: arithmetic; the difference is whether the value being judged already
404: exists anywhere in the simulation before this actor produces it.)
405: 
406: Once the scan above finds no positive trigger — or to confirm one you did
407: find should stay action-shaped rather than dissolve into arithmetic —
408: reason about the requirement in this order:
409: 
410: 1. **Is this fully deterministic?** — a calculation, a consequence, a
411:    bookkeeping write, no new agent judgment involved. → route through
412:    `norms/*.py`, no matter how novel-sounding the rule is. Some rules
413:    really are this simple; many are not — don't assume this is the
414:    common case before checking.
415: 2. **Does an existing action's own `call_fisher_agent()` response schema
416:    already have a field whose value directly answers this specific
417:    requirement** — not a field that could be creatively reinterpreted to
418:    answer it — even if nothing currently enforces it? → still routes
419:    through `norms/*.py`, reading that existing output — no action change
420:    of any kind, new or edited.
421: 3. **Neither of the above** — the norm genuinely requires a new agent
422:    decision/act that no existing action hosts → a new action is required
423:    (Section 5/13).
424: 
425: Never default `new norm → new action`. **Equally, never default `new
426: norm → norms/*.py` because it's cheaper to build.** A `Norm` plugin has
427: no judgment — only arithmetic over values that already exist. If the
428: requirement asks an actor to weigh, decide, inspect, or judge something
429: using information not already reduced to a number or boolean, that is
430: action-shaped by definition, regardless of how much simpler a `norms/`
431: file would be to write — a new action costs five separate artifacts
432: (Section 13) against `norms/`'s one file plus a config entry, and that
433: cost difference is never itself a legitimate reason to pick the cheaper
434: route. Existing actions are never edited to reach outcome 1 or 2 — not
435: the five originally-protected ones, and not one an earlier round of
436: yours created either (Section 13).
437: 
438: **Before treating that five-artifact cost as a reason to defer or skip a
439: genuine new-action requirement, verify the real cost — don't price it
440: from memory.** For the common case (one fisher-agent call per
441: participating agent, optionally granting a role or recording a visible
442: fact from the response), `engine.action_base.SimpleAgentAction` (Section
443: 13) makes the code artifact three small method overrides, not a custom
444: loop — you must have actually read that file (Section 1) before judging
445: otherwise. A real round classified a council/election requirement as
446: needing "new institutional infrastructure" and deferred it without ever
447: opening `engine/action_base.py` to check what that infrastructure
448: actually costs, and without asking the proposer (via
449: `engine.clarify_norm`, Section 5) whether the requirement could be scoped
450: down to something smaller this round. If a requirement is still
451: genuinely larger than one round's budget after actually checking the
452: real cost — a role *plus* a new election action *plus* wiring an
453: existing norm to consult it, say — that is exactly the case for
454: `engine.clarify_norm` to ask about scope, or for implementing the
455: smallest real piece (e.g. the role alone, honestly reported as partial)
456: rather than silently implementing nothing for it (Section 5).
